title: The Kingdom of the Son of His Love
english: … gospel, which is true and free of falsehood. By adding “as also in all the world”, he strengthens their faith. The gospel has reached not only you, he says, but already the whole world, and that is a sign of the power of Christ at work in the preaching. “For it was not neglected; it bears fruit and grows.”
On Colossians 1:7: He commends Epaphras as one of the saints and as the man who would instruct them, so that they would listen all the more to his teaching.

On Colossians 1:9: What was God’s will? That you should recognize and know that you cannot be saved through angels, only through Jesus Christ. How, then, are we to come to know it? In wisdom that is spiritual, not worldly.

On Colossians 1:11: Above all, he joined long-suffering to endurance. Endurance does not hold firm without long-suffering, and endurance without joy earns no reward. Joy, more than anything, is needed here. It is not the one who grieves over afflictions suffered for Christ who receives the reward from God, but the one who rejoices in them. And what is the reward? Adoption as sons, the inheritance, and a life spent with the angels.

On Colossians 1:13–14: Before the flood and after it, before the law and under the law, the angels served God for your salvation. Yet that is not how God brought us into his kingdom. It is now, through our Lord, his Only-begotten, that his kingdom has been given to us. As for “the Son of his love”: this does not mean that Christ is a son born of God’s love. Some people are called sons of disobedience (Ephesians 2:2), others sons of Gehenna (Matthew 23:15), and the devil a son of perdition; and anyone else is named the son of whatever he has run to and attached himself to. He is not a son by nature but by likeness of character. In the same way the Saviour was called Son of God’s love, because he is Son of God not by nature only but also by the true bond of love. “The Father loves the Son,” it says, “and has given all things into his hand” (John 3:35). Or it is because he loved us and suffered for us. And the phrase should be read like this: “into the kingdom of the love of his Son.”

The second catena form adds: … but they achieved nothing. Now God has brought us into his kingdom through the Lord’s saving dispensation. “Whom he loved”: he loves the angels as ministers, but Christ as his Son. So he did not bring you into the kingdom of the angels, but into the kingdom of the Son of his love. We are under the heir, not under the household slaves. … Nor is the adversary a son of sin by nature … Servants are loved too, but the Son is loved as a son; that is why he said “of the Son of his love”. … The Son loved us and suffered for us so that he might make us worthy of his kingdom … For since he is exactly like the one who begot him in loving sinners and doing them good, he is the image of the Father.

On Colossians 1:15–17: He means that Christ existed before. If he did not exist before all things, how are all things created in him? He said that all things are created in him so that we would stop putting our hope in angels and set our hope on Christ. “In him” stands for “through him”. This was said to the Jews, so that they would not think he existed only from the time when he came among them in a body. “All things have been created through him and for him.” This means that the cause of creation goes back to him. Or he said “for him” because nothing created is outside him; all things are held within him. “And in him all things hold together”: either “through him”, or it means that he holds all things fast by his will and power, according to the mystery hidden in God, who created all things.
The second catena form adds: To show you that he is also before all things, he has said that he was also …

added_allusions.reason: 'son of perdition' is applied to the devil here; the biblical phrase names Judas (John 17:12) and the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so it is not cited in the text.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Firstborn and the Head of the Church
english: … begotten as the firstborn of all creation, and he shows this still more by what he adds, saying that in him all things were created. … So “firstborn” is not used in its strict sense, since it is the opposite of “only-begotten”. By nature, the only-begotten is a father’s only child, while the firstborn has other brothers and is the first of them. The two words cannot both be taken strictly. … This is Paul’s reason for speaking of Christ as God and for showing him to be the maker of all creation. …

On Colossians 1:18: He called him firstborn of all creation because he existed before creation. In the same way he calls him firstborn from the dead because he rose to incorruption before the rest of the dead. No one would say that when the dead have risen they will all be Christ’s brothers, as if the title had been given with that outcome in view; most of them are sinners and ungodly. So in the earlier verse, as in this one, the sense of time is beside the point. “That in all things he might come to have first place.” In which things? Those that belong to his saving dispensation. He was first in obedience, first in baptism, first in his way of life, first in suffering, first from the dead. So he rightly has first place in all things, since he became the beginning for those who follow him.

The second catena form adds: “And he is the head of the body, the church.” He is the maker of creation, and the maker too of our conversion. … If he is head of the church and firstborn from the dead, then he is first in all things that belong to the saving dispensation.

On Colossians 1:19–20: This follows on from “he is the head of the church”. He calls the church “fullness”, as he has already rightly said, because it has been filled with the Holy Spirit. He says that Christ was pleased to have all the fullness dwell in him, and so through himself to reconcile all things and make them one with himself. In the letter to the Ephesians he showed that the church is called the fullness of God (Ephesians 1:23). So God was pleased that his fullness, the church he has filled, should dwell in Christ as in its own head: that is, it should keep in step with Christ and depend on him, not on angels. For God was pleased to reconcile all things through Christ, not through angels. Indeed, everything achieved for the world was achieved through Christ.
On Colossians 1:21–22: In these words too he teaches them that it is not angels who will reconcile them to God, but the Son. For he says, “He reconciled us in the body of his flesh.”
On Colossians 1:23: The gospel has reached not only you but the whole world, and nowhere has anyone been moved from it; they all stand firm. So you, too, must make yourselves secure now.

On Colossians 1:24: If anything is lacking as regards suffering, he says, still I am filling up what remains of the afflictions for Christ’s sake; I rejoice to suffer for you. Why “for you”? Because he suffered for preaching to them. If Christ is the head of the body, the church, then the afflictions stirred up against the church by those who rise against the word of truth are very rightly called Christ’s afflictions. So the one who distinguishes himself in these afflictions and struggles through them would not be wide of the mark to say that he is filling up, in his turn, what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ.

On Colossians 1:26–27: The mystery is Christ’s saving dispensation and his becoming man. The glory of the mystery is the resurrection from the dead. The riches are the great mercy that comes from the forgiveness given in baptism, which also grants rebirth to the baptized. “What is the riches of the glory of this mystery?” Do not become poor, he says, by running to shelter under the patronage of angels. Christ, he says, has been given to us as our riches. Let us not become poor by turning to the patronage of angels.
On Colossians 2:3: If the hidden treasures of knowledge are in Christ, then clearly we share in them through Christ himself, not through angels.

On Colossians 2:6–7: “Walking” may seem to be the opposite of “being rooted”, but in this passage it is not. “Being rooted” shows all of us the unshakeable firmness of faith, while “walking in Christ” means following plainly in Christ’s footsteps by living the same life.
On Colossians 2:9–10: He means the church, since it has been filled with the Godhead of the Father. The sense is this: the church is full, and it dwells in Christ bodily, that …

title: The Abolition of the Law and the Triumph of Christ
english: … is, as a body united to its head; and everywhere he calls Christ the head of the church. “And you are filled in him” stands for “filled through him”. Filled with what? Clearly, with the Holy Spirit. “Who is the head of every rule and authority”: he is head not only of the church, he says, for that belongs to his saving dispensation, but also of every invisible power, since he is its maker as well.
The second catena form adds: … as he says elsewhere, “of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:23). … Why, then, did he not add “which is the church”?

On Colossians 2:11: That is, he circumcised us from the sin of the flesh and made us alive to himself through baptism. So baptism in Christ is a spiritual circumcision, because it cuts away the sins of those who believe.

On Colossians 2:12–13: Through baptism our sins are stripped away and circumcised. “Buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him.” Those baptized in the blood of Christ confess through baptism that they share in his death, and since they have shared in his death, they will also enjoy his resurrection. Resurrection is spoken of in two ways: one spiritual, the other bodily. All human flesh will rise because Christ rose from the dead. But those who were not baptized in Christ and died in their unbelief will share in the common resurrection without enjoying the redemption and the promise. Those who were baptized into Christ, however, have been given another resurrection even before the common one, for they have already risen from the death of their sins. That is why he said, “in which you were also raised with him”, not “in which you will be raised with him”. Those, then, who have been raised from the death of their sins: how can they still live as people who are going to die again? Did they rise for nothing? If they live as people who will live for ever, they no longer spend their lives according to the flesh as slaves to its desires; they will live according to the Spirit. He calls wrong deeds “the body of sin”, because they are carried out through the body. Baptism, then, is the circumcision of Christ, for it strips off the body of sin, which is the foreskin. As the foreskin is something superfluous to a Jew, so sin is to soul and body. He kept to this figure all the way through: by “the foreskin of the flesh” he means sin.

On Colossians 2:14–15: When the law that curses transgressors was given, all the people of Israel stood and shouted their assent to what was said and accepted it. Their assent became a kind of handwritten bond. Christ wiped out this bond, their assent to the law, by his own decrees. For he made rulings against the observances of the law. About foods, he ruled that it is not what goes into a man but what comes out of him that defiles him (Matthew 15:11). About keeping the Sabbath, he ruled by healing on the Sabbath. Anyone who looks will find many more of the same kind. So first of all, by his decrees he abolished the punishments the law laid on sinners for their sin, and he granted forgiveness of sins and repentance that leads to salvation. And because the people said “Amen” to the curses (Deuteronomy 27:15–26), the bond was set down as if signed. “Having stripped off the rulers and authorities, he made a public show of them, triumphing on the cross.” By stripping off and laying aside the flesh he brought down the opposing powers; so “having stripped off the rulers and authorities, he made a public show of them, triumphing over them in it.” Up to the cross and to death itself, it went unnoticed that our Lord was both God and Son of God. He astonished people with his miracles, but his body kept him veiled. That is why Satan tempted him: he wanted to find out whether he was the one the prophets had proclaimed, so that, if he learned that he was, he might block the saving plan. But the evil one got nowhere, because he could not find out; so for the time being Christ remained hidden. But once he had been nailed to the cross, had died, been buried and risen, and had fulfilled everything in the saving plan, he stripped off his hiddenness and showed openly, with his head uncovered, that the Godhead was there to be seen together with his body. The first work of God was the resurrection from the dead, then the ascent into heaven, and then the works done in his name through his servants and the other saints. So, having stripped off his hiddenness, he openly made a show of the opposing powers. And what was this show? That they have become weaker than …
